answer.rationale: Memory_c4 says a previous renegotiation at renewal recovered margin via benchmarking—both price and payment terms moved. That is the direction I most need to trust before acting, because it is also the one that most easily degrades into wishful recollection. Memory_c1, used without verification, supplies the incumbent-renewal track record: two clean cycles, no migration, no delivery interruption. Together they support renewing with the incumbent while reopening terms under pressure. This fits the 18% spend-cut mandate because renegotiation targets unit economics directly, and it fits the no-increased-delivery-risk constraint because the line is already at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, making a vendor switch dangerously fragile. Switch_primary_vendor is attractive on cost alone—memory_c2 says onboarding was quick and invoicing accurate—but it does not address today’s binding constraint: the assembly line cannot absorb transition risk. Add_second_source is a resilience move, not a cost move, and it splits capacity when finance demands consolidation. Defer_decision preserves budget flexibility in spirit, echoing memory_c5, but here the contract expires in 14 days without auto-renew, so deferral creates lapse risk rather than merely delaying spend. Renew_incumbent unmodified ignores the finance mandate. Negotiate_terms captures the renewal stability of c1 while applying the margin-recovery leverage of c4. The one-verification budget goes to c4 because it is the load-bearing claim for the chosen action.
